Make sure you check your local laws for gun powder handling / storage, and definitely do tons of research so you don't blow yourself up.

You have a lot to learn and it's all important. Take your time and ask for help when you need it.

Remember that you'll be loading thousands of rounds over the course of your life, and your tolerance for a serious error is zero percent. One bad round can ruin a gun, and damage you, too.

My advice is to understand, right at the start, that you are not and will never be perfect. You can make up the difference with good habits that keep the consequences of the inevitable mistakes small.

One of the easiest ways to blow up a gun is with a double charge of powder. The next easiest way is with a correct charge of the wrong powder. Sometimes, using the wrong primer or the wrong projectile is enough to push a warm load over the edge.

You can prevent most of these problems by storing your powder, primers, and bullets in a separate room. When you want to load your .308 with 180 grain bullets, you go into the room, select the right powder, the right bullets, the right primers, and take them to your press. When you are done you put them all back, and grab what you need for the next batch. You'll never have the wrong things within reach while you are reloading.

When you pick a recipe, use one that fills the case, or comes close to filling the case, with powder. Now you'll never double-charge it. This can be hard for rounds like the .357, a powder like Bullseye barely covers the bottom. Use trailboss or something similar whenever you can.

Get comfortable using a micrometer. It's a skill that's easy to get wrong. If you can't measure the same item five times and get the same measurement, your technique need attention. Your case length, neck thickness, and base thickness all matter.

The best load is usually not the hottest load. You want good accuracy, good case life, reliable feeding and extraction. If you really feel like you need more power out of your .308, get a 30-06, or a .300 winchester. When you're in it for the long haul, there's no point in pushing your luck. You will make small mistakes.

Finally, use your computer to print one recipe per page, in a format you like that's easy to read. It's surprisingly easy to read one number off of one row and the next number off a different row, when assembling components. If it's all on one page that entire class of hazard is eliminated.

I too would recommend starting out with a good single stage press by RCBS or Hornady. You're going to learn the little details that make for safe and reliable ammunition manufacturing better by going slow at first.

The number one, absolutely most important detail a beginning reloader must pay attention to is powder charges, and it's very easy to make mistakes on a progressive press. A loaded cartridge without a powder charge (squib load) is just as dangerous as an over charged one when fired.

With a single stage press and all of your charged cases in a shell block, you can hover overhead with a flashlight and inspect each case for powder levels.
